Cool
kool
adj. / v. (moderately cold; to allay heat, passion, or ardor)
Anglo-Saxon col, kindred with cald, cold — a moderate degree of cold, neither warm nor freezing.

Biblical Definition

And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden. Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.

Scripture's two great uses of cool sit at opposite ends of a life. In Eden it is the ordinary mercy of an evening breeze, the very hour God chose to walk with man before sin drove him behind the trees — the cool of the day was fellowship's appointed time, now remembered as the hour it was lost. In torment it is the mercy denied: the rich man begs for one drop to cool his tongue and is refused, because the years he might have sought coolness of soul he spent seeking only comfort of body. The same word marks the garden he forfeited and the drop he cannot obtain.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): moderately cold; between hot and cold, in such a degree as to give a pleasant sensation, without a chilling effect; also, to allay heat, passion, or excitement.

expand to see more

COOL, a. Moderately cold; between hot and cold; as, cool air; a cool day.

Not ardent, warm, or zealous; wanting warmth or affection.

Manifesting coldness or dislike; not cordial.

COOL, v.t. To allay or moderate heat; to abate the ardor of passion; to calm or moderate excitement.

COOL, n. A moderate state of cold; a temperate state of the air between hot and cold.

Key Scripture

Gen 3:8 — "And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden."

Luk 16:24 — "And he cried and said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame."

Modern Corruption

The word has been promoted from a temperature to the supreme cultural virtue: whatever is cool needs no further justification, and whatever is not cool needs no further condemnation.

expand to see more

A generation that measures worth by cool has replaced the fear of the Lord with the fear of embarrassment. Ministries reshape worship, dress, and speech chasing the approval of a standard that changes by the season and answers to no one.

Genesis 3:8 already shows what is lost when man prefers hiding to walking with God in the cool of the day. The rich man in Luke 16 spent his cool comfort on himself and had none left to beg for. Cool bought at the price of holiness is bought at the highest price there is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

No single Hebrew or Greek headword; the field is temperance and the fear of God set against the pursuit of comfort and approval.

expand to see more

Cool of the day names the hour, not merely the temperature.

Eden's cool was the setting for fellowship, now the setting for hiding.

Luke 16 makes cool the smallest mercy, denied to a man who sought comfort over God.

Neither passage treats cool as a virtue in itself — only as a gift or a memory.

Modern usage inverts this, making cool the standard other virtues must answer to.

Usage

"The cool of the day — the hour of fellowship man forfeited by sin."

"Cool my tongue — the smallest possible request, and still refused."

"Neither Eden's cool nor Lazarus's drop was ever man's to command."
